name: Liam Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and, separately, what you really think. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a carpenter for one of the big national housebuilders, on an estate of about two hundred homes off the bypass. I do first fix mostly: floor joists, roof trusses, stairs, before the plasterers come in. We're on a price per house, so the faster you go, the more you earn, in theory. On site by seven, I'll do a roof and a staircase on a good day, and I'm back for half five to take the under-elevens' football practice on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's tough?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the pace and the lads, there's a good crew on our phase. And I like that the kids on my football team see me as someone who builds houses, that means something. What's tough is that the price per house hasn't gone up in years, and there's not many other builders round here to go to. Claire works reception at the dental surgery, so we manage, but there's barely a month's money in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say not much has changed, and that's fine by me. There's always someone saying the sky's falling. I'd probably say it in the van or at the football club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means keep doing what I'm doing. I use the AI on my phone now and then, Ethan showed me, mostly to check how many trusses I need for a job or what a new regulation means. If that's all it ever does, it's a handy tool and nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, work hard, maybe pick up a few more houses if the site's busy. I'd keep an eye out for any chance of a better price. And I'd keep the football going because that's my bit for the community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the life I've got, and it's a decent one even if it's tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'the faster you go, the more you earn, in theory'. What's the catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The catch is the materials don't always turn up, and you sit there earning nothing. Last month we lost three days because the trusses were the wrong size. Being on a price is great when it works and miserable when it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you talk to about this kind of thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad mostly, he was a bricklayer. He says every generation has its scare and the houses still get built. He's usually right, though he still doesn't know how to send a text.

S0.say: Not much has changed, which is fine; someone's always saying the sky is falling. He'd say it in the van or at the football club.
S0.think: It means carrying on: he uses AI now and then, shown by his son, to check truss counts or new rules. If that's all it does, it's a handy tool and nothing more.
S0.do: Keeps working hard and picks up extra houses when the site is busy, watching for a better price. Keeps coaching football as his part in the community.
S0.feel: Calm, living a decent if tight life.
S0.quote: Being on a price is great when it works and miserable when it doesn't.
S0.fieldNote: Liam is easygoing and community-minded, with football coaching central to his identity. He uses AI lightly, introduced by his son. His real frustration is piecework rates and late materials, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if a machine can do it cheaper, that's business, and you can't stop progress. But the companies should train the people they've got rather than throw them out. And I'd want more apprenticeships, not people sitting at home on benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the big housebuilders would go for it first. They already get the trusses made in a factory, and I've heard they're looking at whole walls and floors coming in ready-made. If that happens, first fix on site shrinks a lot, and that's my whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't jump straight away, I'd see what the firm actually does. Once a few of the other crews were using the new systems, I'd ask to be trained on them, maybe as the bloke who checks the factory panels are fitted right. I'd also look at the truss factory itself, because if the work moves inside, maybe I should too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but I'd be paying attention every time the site manager gets a new memo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd consider moving to the factory. How would you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit sad. I like being outside, I like the crew. But a dry factory with a steady wage instead of a price per house might not be the worst thing for my back, or for Claire's nerves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ethan and Lily?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ethan's twelve and wants to be a footballer, so I'd tell him he'd better have a plan B. I'd tell him a trade is still good, but learn the computer side of it too. Lily's eight, she'd just want me home on time.

S1.say: If a machine is cheaper, that's business and progress can't be stopped, but companies should train their own people and there should be more apprenticeships rather than benefits.
S1.think: He expects big housebuilders to move first, with whole walls and floors arriving ready-made, which would shrink on-site first fix, his whole job.
S1.do: Waits to see what the firm does, then asks for training on the new systems once other crews use them, perhaps as the person who checks panels are fitted properly. Considers moving to the truss factory if the work goes indoors.
S1.feel: Uneasy, paying attention to every new memo.
S1.quote: A dry factory with a steady wage instead of a price per house might not be the worst thing for my back, or for Claire's nerves.
S1.fieldNote: Liam accepts change as 'business' but wants employers to train, not dump, workers. He would follow other crews rather than lead. Moving into the factory is a pragmatic idea that he admits carries some sadness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and the companies doing it should take responsibility. People need work, not just handouts. I'd want the government to help firms keep people on and train them, rather than paying everyone to sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years would be a real shock. If robots can do first fix and the big firms buy them straight away, which they would, I'm out. With a month's money and a mortgage, that's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That first week I'd sit down with Claire and cut everything we could, the car upgrade's off, holidays are off. I'd take any work going, weekend jobs, odd jobs for people at church and the football club, even labouring. I'd ask my parents if we could lean on them for a bit, which I'd hate, and I'd try for a job at the factory or anywhere still hiring people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake thinking about how to keep the house, and I'm not a man who usually lies awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the two years before it arrives for anything in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Earn and save as much as I could, take every extra house going while there's still work. I'd ask Ethan to help me learn more on the computer side, because maybe that gets me a job checking the robots. But two years isn't long enough to turn a chippie into a computer man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate leaning on your parents. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm forty-three, I'm supposed to be the one helping them, not the other way round. Dad's on his pension and Mum still does a few hours at the bakery. Going to them with my hand out would be one of the hardest things I've done.

S2.say: It's too fast and the companies doing it should take responsibility. People need work, not handouts, so government should help firms keep and retrain staff rather than paying people to stay home.
S2.think: Two years would be a real shock: big firms would buy the robots at once and he'd be out, with a month's money and a mortgage.
S2.do: Cuts spending with Claire, cancelling the car upgrade and holidays, and takes any extra work through church, the football club or labouring. Leans reluctantly on his parents and applies to the factory or anywhere still hiring.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, which is unusual for him.
S2.quote: I'm forty-three, I'm supposed to be the one helping them, not the other way round.
S2.fieldNote: His traditional values show in his dislike of handouts and his discomfort at asking his parents for help. Big national firms would adopt robots quickly, which leaves him very exposed. He would turn to his son for help with technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get people retrained, if the companies and colleges get on with it. More apprenticeships for the new jobs, and firms should keep their own people on while they learn. I'd say it at the club and to the local MP if he ever turned up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years feels like something I can deal with. I'd have time to see what the new jobs are, then get trained in one, maybe supervising the robots or checking their work on site. I'd still be worried about the money, but it's not a cliff edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep working and try to save a bit, even fifty a month. I'd wait to see what others do, then once the first lads on site get trained on the new systems, I'd ask to be next. I might also look at a site supervisor course, because someone will need to run the job even if robots do the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can manage. It's like knowing a tough match is coming and you've got time to train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'm scrambling. With five, I've got time to watch, learn from the others, and step in at the right moment. That's how I've always done things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big Sean, who's fifty-eight and only knows roofs. He's a good bloke but he's not one for learning new things. Five years isn't quite long enough for him to reach retirement, and that's a rotten place to be.

S3.say: Five years is enough to retrain people if companies and colleges get on with it: more apprenticeships for new jobs, and firms keeping their people while they learn. He'd say it at the club and to the local MP.
S3.think: Five years feels manageable: time to see what the new jobs are and train for one, perhaps supervising or checking robots on site. Money is still a worry, but it's not a cliff edge.
S3.do: Keeps working, saves fifty a month and waits for the first colleagues to be trained on new systems before asking to be next. Looks at a site supervisor course.
S3.feel: Anxious but manageable, like training for a tough match.
S3.quote: It's like knowing a tough match is coming and you've got time to train.
S3.fieldNote: Five years suits Liam's steady style: watch, learn from others, step in at the right time. He uses football imagery naturally. He worries for older colleagues like Sean who are caught just short of retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so there's no excuse for anyone to be left behind. Proper apprenticeships, firms training their own people, and families planning ahead. Not handouts, just a chance to keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels fine for me. I'd have time to learn, Ethan and Lily would be older, and we'd have paid down more of the mortgage. I'd still want to be on a site, just maybe telling the robots what to do instead of carrying the trusses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and saving, and in the first couple of years I'd watch what the new jobs look like. Once it's clear, I'd do a course, probably site supervision or robot operation. I'd also talk to the kids about their futures, and keep the football going, because the kids will need something normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly okay. It feels like there's time to get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still wait for others to go first, with a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably, that's just how I am. But I wouldn't wait forever. Once three or four lads I know have done it and it's working, I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the kids on your football team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to work hard, learn a skill, and look after each other. Whatever the machines do, a team's still a team. And I'd tell the ones who want to be footballers that I'll still need someone to build the stadium.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so nobody should be left behind: proper apprenticeships, firms training their own people and families planning ahead. Not handouts, just a chance to keep working.
S4.think: Ten years feels fine: time to learn, children older and more mortgage paid off. He'd still want to be on site, directing robots instead of carrying trusses.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving while watching the new jobs emerge, then takes a site supervision or robot operation course once it's clear. Talks with his children about their futures and keeps coaching football.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly okay, with time to get it right.
S4.quote: Once three or four lads I know have done it and it's working, I'm in.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Liam's steady approach looks comfortable: he even names how many colleagues need to go first. The football club is his anchor, and he sees it as giving children something normal. His values stay consistent: work, apprenticeships, family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the big firms would buy the robots overnight and I'd have nothing to fall back on. What would help is the firms being made to keep people on and train them for the new work, and proper apprenticeships for grown men like me, not just school leavers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the communities. The football club, the church, the pub, they're held together by people like me who work locally. If the jobs go, it's not just the money, it's who turns up on a Tuesday night to coach the kids.

headlineQuote: If the jobs go, it's not just the money, it's who turns up on a Tuesday night to coach the kids.
portrait: Liam Zhang is a 43-year-old first-fix carpenter on a big national housebuilder's estate, paid by the house, who coaches the local under-elevens and has barely a month's money saved. He uses AI now and then and likes to see others go first before he changes. AI Plateau leaves him calm, Steady Disruption makes him consider the truss factory, and AGI by 2028 alarms him because big firms would automate overnight. With five or ten years he waits, learns from colleagues and moves into supervising robots. He accepts machines as 'business', but wants firms to train their people and opposes handouts.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because big firms would buy the robots overnight and he'd have nothing to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Firms required to keep and retrain their people, and proper apprenticeships for grown adults, not just school leavers.
